articles.title: Israel’s elections 2026 explained in maps and charts
articles.summary: Israelis vote on October 27 in the sixth election since 2019. Here’s how the system works and who gets left out.
articles.body:
Israelis go to the polls on October 27 to elect the 26th Knesset, in the first general vote since the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza and the wars on Lebanon and Iran.

Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history, with 19 years in office, is seeking another term while standing trial on corruption charges. His Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads are locked in a close race with a Jewish-led opposition bloc, with neither side appearing on track to win an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament.

About 7.3 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. Most polling stations open from 7am to 10pm, and anyone still queuing when they close is entitled to vote. Election day is a national holiday.

Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, which sits for a four-year term. There are no term limits for a prime minister.

Israelis vote for a party, not a candidate.

A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats and no party has ever won that outright. Finishing first does not guarantee power. Parties then have 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days, to assemble a coalition reaching 61. If nobody manages it, the country votes again.

Seats are shared out in proportion to each party’s share of the national vote, so a party winning 30 percent of votes takes roughly 30 percent of seats. The votes for parties failing to secure 3.25 percent are discarded, which explains why small parties routinely merge before every election.

About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in this election, but they are not the only adults living under the government they choose.

Roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no vote in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status.

Jewish Israelis and Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million, can vote. So can adult settlers among the more than 750,000 Israelis living in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, who help elect the parliament that legislates over the land they live on.

Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem hold Israeli residency, not citizenship. They can vote for Jerusalem’s city council but not for the Knesset.

The result is a sharp anomaly in the occupied West Bank, where a settler votes and a Palestinian family living nearby, under the same military authority, does not.

Most Israeli citizens living abroad also cannot vote, because Israel has no general absentee ballot and requires voters to be physically in the country on election day. Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception, casting their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.

Israelis are dealing with a series of domestic and international issues this election cycle, including:

October 7 security failures – Three years on, the government is yet to form a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-headed attack led to the killing of some 1,200 people, with about 250 taken captive. Israel launched the genocidal war against Palestinians in the wake of the attack, killing at least 74,000 people and leaving most of the besieged territory in ruins.

Ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions – Supporters of the exemptions say they protect full-time Torah study, but critics argue they place an unfair military burden on everyone else.

Judicial reform – Netanyahu’s push to curb the Supreme Court’s powers, which sparked mass protests before the war on Gaza, remains a deep fault line. Critics see it as a threat to democracy, while supporters argue that the court has overstepped its authority.

War and security – The public wants stability but remains wary of concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. Netanyahu promised “total victory”, but Hamas and Hezbollah remain operational.

Cost of living – High prices and modest wages are being further squeezed by soaring defence spending. Since 2023, Israel’s defence budget has doubled, increasing pressure on public finances.

Netanyahu’s coalition held 60 of the Knesset’s 120 seats when parliament dissolved in July. It comprised Likud with 32 seats, Shas with 11, Religious Zionism with seven, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit with six, and New Hope with four. Shas left the government in July 2025 but remained in the coalition and New Hope will merge into Likud for this election.

The opposition held 59 seats: Yesh Atid with 24, Blue and White with eight, United Torah Judaism with seven, Yisrael Beiteinu with six, Hadash-Taal and Raam with five each and Labor with four. Noam’s single seat was unaffiliated.

Netanyahu is seeking re-election while facing a trial on corruption charges, which he denies.

His far-right coalition is up against a bloc comprising of four major Jewish-led opposition parties, whose leaders have signed a declaration promising not to attack each other ahead of the vote and to join forces in forming a government after the polls.

Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister, with his new Yashar party evenly matched with Likud in the opinion polls.

The opposition alliance includes the Together list, led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.

Other key players include far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, the ultra-Orthodox parties, and the Arab-majority lists Ra’am and the Joint List.

Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List from the election, but the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bans on October 2, ruling that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold for exclusion.

Sami Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel who leads Balad, one of the parties in the Joint List, withdrew from the race after the court signalled that a majority of its judges would uphold his disqualification.

The Arab-led parties could hold the balance of power after the vote, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them.

October 27 will be Israel’s sixth national vote since 2019, but the first in 38 years to arrive at the natural end of a full Knesset term.

The instability began in April 2019, when Netanyahu’s Likud party and Benny Gantz’s Blue and White party tied on 35 seats each. A second vote that September produced another deadlock, with Blue and White on 33 and Likud on 32, and neither round yielded a coalition able to reach a majority.

A third election in March 2020 gave Likud 36 seats to Blue and White’s 33, and produced a Netanyahu-Gantz unity government that collapsed within a year. In March 2021, Likud won 30 seats to Yesh Atid’s 17, but an eight-party coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that also included Ra’am, an Arab party, ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run. It lasted a year.

Netanyahu returned in November 2022, with Likud on 32 and Yesh Atid on 24, at the head of what has been described as Israel’s most right-wing government. Polls now show neither bloc clearly reaching 61.

The state of Israel has had 14 prime ministers since its foundation in 1948. Netanyahu is by far the longest-serving, with 19 years in three separate stints: 1996 to 1999, 2009 to 2021 and from 2022 to now

Only David Ben-Gurion, who led the country from 1948 to 1954 and again from 1955 to 1963, comes close.

Whatever happens on October 27, Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in.

articles.title: In 2022, Pennsylvania salvager Paul Brown paid $6,000 for church windows; one year later, experts identified Tiffany glass, and the pair sold for $200,000
articles.summary: Discover how Paul Brown turned a $6,000 church window purchase into a $200,000 sale after experts identified them as valuable Tiffany glass. A tale of hidden treasures and legal challenges surrounding ownership.
articles.body: Rarely do old city churches enjoy a peaceful retirement. Buildings change hands, floors are torn up, and anything sufficiently dusty is sold off in a bundle when congregations decline, and maintenance begins to exceed revenue. Most old fixtures are precisely what they appear to be: worn and weathered. Occasionally, however, something valuable escapes because no one stopped to take a careful look.That almost happened in a big Gothic church in West Philadelphia, where two giant round windows had hung above the benches for over a hundred years, covered in a thick layer of grime. In November 2022, Pennsylvania salvager Paul Brown bought the windows as part of a larger sale for $6,000. After Brown contacted Freeman’s for help with the damaged glass, specialists identified the windows as work by Tiffany Studios. They sold at auction on May 18, 2023, for $200,000 before the buyer’s premium, or $252,000 including fees.The sale did not immediately deliver a financial return to Brown. He reportedly spent more than $100,000 on removal and restoration, and a bank later challenged ownership of the windows, leaving the auction proceeds frozen. The dispute raised questions about who legally owned fixtures removed from a historic building.A bargain in West PhiladelphiaThe church stands at the intersection of 50th Street and Baltimore Avenue in West Philadelphia. Built for the congregation of St Paul’s Presbyterian, dedicated in 1901 and extended in 1905, it moved to Hickman Temple AME Church in 1972. New owner, Pastor William Brownlee Sr. of Emmanuel Christian Centre, purchased the 15,000-square-foot property in 2022 and started modernising the space, which included removing a lot of old fixtures.Paul Brown, an architectural salvager based in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, has spent decades rescuing historic building materials and fixtures. He learned about the windows through a Facebook Marketplace listing and was told they needed to be removed before workers demolished them. He paid $6,000 for the windows and some other fixtures bundled with the windows in November of 2022. Removing the two windows from their stone frames took about a month of painstaking work, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer.No one involved knew what they were in for. In his world, Tiffany always meant lights, never windows, Brown has told us. Even local preservationists overlooked it. The 35-page submission the University City Historical Society submitted in 2020 when it nominated the church for historic classification included nothing at all about Tiffany.What the grime was hidingBrown wrapped the windows in packing blankets and called Freeman’s to find out how to fix the shattered and loose glass. They identified the pieces as being from St Paul’s and Tiffany Studios, whose 1910 list of commissions mentions the church under the heading “Wanamaker Memorial”. John Wanamaker, a Philadelphia department-store magnate and church supporter, may have helped arrange the commission. Tiffany’s 1910 records list the church under the heading “Wanamaker Memorial,” although the surviving record does not establish his exact role in commissioning the windows.Each of the windows is around 90 inches wide and is made up of eight petals, eight kites and a central quatrefoil. One is concentrated on a crown and the other on a dove. On one of them, the lot description on Freeman’s own site also mentions a dedication from the church’s Pansy Bible Class. The glass is layered and diversified, with ripple, streaky, mottled, opalescent and acid-etched pieces, some of them plated on the back for depth. Julie Sloan, a stained glass consultant, writes for the auction house that the design is read as a single day, with deep purple night on the outer edge, a thin band of turquoise dawn, and brighter golds and greens closing in to the core.So why didn’t anyone notice? Years of filth and grime undoubtedly obscured the telling elements; the newspapers that marked the church’s consecration didn’t mention Tiffany by name, and the firm’s contemporary renown is grounded in its lamps. But the studio was a behemoth of cathedral glass in its day. By the 1880s, the Tiffany Glass Company was the greatest manufacturer of stained glass windows in the United States, the Met adds. The auction generated $252,000 including fees, but that amount did not represent Brown’s profit: he had reportedly spent more than $100,000 on removal and restoration, and the proceeds were subsequently frozen amid the ownership dispute.Auction day and a legal messThe windows were auctioned at Freeman’s in Philadelphia on May 18, 2023. Each sold for a hammer price of $100,000 to an anonymous buyer, below the low estimate of $150,000 per window. Including the buyer’s premium, the final price was $126,000 per window, or $252,000 for the pair, according to The Philadelphia Inquirer.Then came the hitch. Within days of the sale, a law firm representing Fulton Bank, which held the mortgage on the church, argued that the windows were covered by the mortgage lien and therefore belonged to the bank. Freeman had acknowledged earlier that Brown was the legal owner of the windows and held the revenues. As of August 2023, Brown still hadn’t received any money; however, he stated he would split a portion of the profits with the church’s pastor, the Inquirer reported.The dispute showed how the removal of historic fixtures can raise complicated ownership questions, particularly when a building is subject to a mortgage. The auction proceeds remained frozen while the competing claims were addressed. Brown initially sought advice on repairing damaged glass. The inquiry led to the identification of two Tiffany Studios rose windows that had remained in the church for more than a century.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1801, Paul Revere bought a home near Boston; 220 years later, renovators found a rare family sign in its attic, and the artifacts sold for $20,000
articles.summary: In a remarkable discovery, renovators found rare artifacts associated with Paul Revere's family in the attic of a home in Canton, Massachusetts. The collection, including a unique trade sign linked to Revere's son, sold at auction for $20,000, far exceeding expectations.
articles.body: Renovators were working on a house in Canton, Massachusetts, when they discovered a collection of artifacts that were associated with Paul Revere's family in an attic wall in 2021. The objects included a black trade sign that bore the name of Revere's son, Joseph W. Revere, along with letters, tools and personal belongings that were connected to the family. The collection was sold as a single lot by an auction house for $20,000 on December 11, 2021, which far exceeded the auctioneer's expectations. John McInnis had expected a sale that fell below $8,000, while the auction website estimated that the collection would fetch between $1,000 and $2,000.A family trade sign attracted biddersA trade sign that was painted black with gold-leaf lettering was one of the most prominent objects in the collection, which carried the name Joseph W. Revere, Paul Revere's son, and was believed to be linked with a business that was operated by the Revere family in Canton. The other objects included wrought-iron calipers, a turned wooden handle, a key, a sewing valet that was made from silk and leather, letters and an account book that belonged to Revere's descendants and daughter-in-law.The company that handled the auction was McInnis, who said that the objects had a historical connection that increased their value, with the auction attracting online, telephone and in-person bidders, and an unidentified online bidder ultimately winning the lot. McInnis told The Boston Globe that early American trade signs typically sold for between $500 and $5,000, based on their condition and appearance. He said that the association with the Revere family made the collection a lot more desirable.Why the Canton property matteredPaul Revere purchased a property in Canton in 1801, according to the Associated Press, and later established the Revere Copper Company on the land. The house where renovators found the objects was believed to have belonged to the Revere family. The artifacts were discovered behind a wall in the attic during renovation work, and their location had kept them out of view, although the available reports do not establish when they were placed there.The collection's historical connection linked the objects to a documented family rather than leaving them as unidentified antiques, which was important to the auction, and the trade sign, in particular, carried a name that could be associated with Revere's descendants. The National Park Service identifies Revere as a master silversmith, engraver, industrialist and messenger during the American Revolution, who became widely known for his ride on the night of April 18, 1775, when he helped warn Patriot leaders of the approaching British forces before the battles of Lexington and Concord. His work as an artisan and businessman continued after the Revolution.Revere’s later enterprises included a foundry and copper mill, with his industrial activities becoming an important part of his career, and the Canton property was connected to this phase of his life. The recovered collection belonged to a later period of the family's history, but its exact age and the circumstances that surrounded its storage were not established fully in the published accounts. The sign's association with Joseph W. Revere and the family documents helped auctioneers identify the lot's historical provenance.The winning bidder remained unidentified, and the reports did not specify where the artifacts would go after the sale. The auction concluded on December 11, 2021, almost two centuries after Revere purchased the Canton property. The objects had emerged during renovation work, and their family connections helped determine the price they ultimately fetched.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2022, a Nashville developer bought a vacant lot, but the city held its building permit for four years while weighing a future road; a federal appeals court has now revived its lawsuit over the freeze
articles.summary: A Nashville property developer has won a significant legal reprieve after a federal appeals court revived its lawsuit against the city over a building
articles.body: A Nashville property developer has won a significant legal reprieve after a federal appeals court revived its lawsuit against the city over a building permit that remained on hold for four years. The dispute began in 2022, when SW Nashville EB Owner, LLC, bought a vacant parcel and sought permission to develop it, only for local authorities to suspend the application while considering a possible future road. According to the Pacific Legal Foundation, which represents the developer, the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit overturned a lower court's dismissal on August 14, 2026, allowing the legal challenge to proceed. The ruling raises broader questions about government planning powers and the constitutional protection of private property.Why Nashville's development hold became a legal disputeSW Nashville purchased a four-acre property in Nashville's East Bank district in the spring of 2022. The company planned to remove a dilapidated building on the site and construct an apartment complex, according to the court record. It applied for standard construction permits, arguing that its proposed development complied with the applicable zoning requirements.However, Nashville's Metropolitan Government, commonly known as Metro, placed an indefinite hold on development applications affecting the property. The city was assessing possible routes for a major future roadway that could require part of the developer's land. The proposed road was still under consideration, but the permit freeze prevented the company from moving forward with its plans. The developer argued that it was left bearing the costs of ownership, including property taxes, maintenance and insurance, without being able to develop or sell the land.Pacific Legal Foundation stated that the restrictions had caused substantial financial losses. Its case page put the company's accumulated taxes and maintenance expenses at more than $8.2 million. The figure reflects the legal organisation's account of the developer's losses, rather than a final court finding on compensation.How the developer challenged the city's decisionSW Nashville argued that keeping its property undevelopable for years, without formally rejecting the permit or acquiring the land, amounted to an unconstitutional taking. The company filed its lawsuit in May 2024, challenging the city's actions under the Takings and Due Process Clauses of the US Constitution, as well as the Takings Clause of the Tennessee Constitution. The case was subsequently transferred to federal court.The Fifth Amendment prohibits the government from taking private property for public use without just compensation. Although eminent domain allows authorities to acquire land for qualifying public projects, the Constitution requires compensation when a taking occurs. The developer's argument centred on whether a government can effectively prevent the use of private property indefinitely while deciding whether it might need that land for a future public project.The case was initially dismissed by the US District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. The lower court concluded that the developer's claims were premature because the city had not reached a final decision on the permit application, leaving the claims unripe for judicial review. SW Nashville appealed, arguing that the indefinite hold itself had already prevented development and caused measurable harm.What the Sixth Circuit decidedIn its August 14, 2026, decision in SW Nashville EB Owner, LLC v. Metropolitan Government of Nashville & Davidson County, the Sixth Circuit reversed the lower court's dismissal and sent the case back for further proceedings. The appeals court determined that the city's continuing development hold constituted a definitive decision for the purpose of deciding whether the developer's claims were ready for judicial review. The company did not have to wait indefinitely for a formal permit rejection when the existing restriction had already barred development.The court considered the practical effect of the city's actions, rather than treating the absence of a final written decision as sufficient reason to prevent the lawsuit from proceeding. Its ruling addressed the question of whether the claims were ripe for review, meaning whether the dispute had developed sufficiently for a court to consider it. Importantly, the appeals court did not finally establish that Nashville had violated the Constitution or order the city to pay compensation. Instead, it reversed the dismissal and remanded the case, allowing the lower court to continue considering the dispute and the remaining legal issues. The case will now return to the lower court, where unresolved issues, including statute-of-limitations arguments and qualified immunity, remain to be considered.What the ruling could mean for property ownersThe decision highlights a difficult balance between public infrastructure planning and private property rights. Cities need time to evaluate road networks, transport projects and other infrastructure requirements. However, prolonged restrictions can create serious financial consequences for owners whose land remains unusable while plans are being considered.The ruling does not prevent governments from planning future roads or acquiring land through lawful eminent-domain procedures. Rather, it indicates that an indefinite development freeze can be sufficiently definitive to allow a property owner's constitutional claims to be heard, even without a formal permit denial. The case could therefore matter to property owners facing similar restrictions, particularly where authorities prevent development while considering a possible future public project. Its ultimate impact will depend on how the lower court resolves the remaining issues.For SW Nashville, the immediate outcome is that its lawsuit can move forward after years of uncertainty. Whether the city must ultimately provide compensation, and whether the developer's constitutional claims succeed on their merits, remain unresolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: South Korea to pull more embassy staff from Ukraine after POW row
articles.summary: Earlier this month, South Korea recalled its ambassador from Kyiv after Zelenskyy disclosed the prisoner transfer.
articles.body:
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs says it will withdraw additional embassy personnel from Ukraine following Kyiv’s lack of “constructive response” in a dispute about North Korean prisoners of war (POWs).

Seoul had told Kyiv of its position via multiple channels but had not received a sufficient response from Ukraine, ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said on Tuesday.

Earlier this month, South Korea recalled its ambassador from Kyiv after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to the South.

The disclosure angered Seoul, which said the operation should have remained confidential to protect the soldiers’ families in North Korea.

“This measure was taken because we judged it necessary to facilitate an amicable resolution of the issue and restore trust between the two countries,” Park told a regular press briefing, without saying how many staff members would leave.

A charge d’affaires would stay on in Kyiv to maintain diplomatic communication along with all consular staff to protect South Korean nationals, Park added.

Persistent threats of air strikes across Ukraine had also made it difficult to ensure staff safety, he said.

Seoul previously summoned the Ukrainian ambassador and threatened unspecified “further measures”.

Ukraine has insisted that “diplomacy must prevail over emotions” in relations between the countries, and also said Kyiv considered “the situation resolved”.

South Korea’s Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said earlier this month that Ukraine had sent a message that “included words of apology” over Zelenskyy’s disclosure, but it fell short of “the level” Seoul had in mind.

Under South Korea’s constitution, all North Koreans are considered citizens of the Republic of Korea, as the country is officially known, and those who reach its territory and seek to defect are generally allowed to stay.

articles.title: Alberta votes overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada, projections suggest
articles.summary: The vote has been hailed by Prime Minister Mark Carney as "a clear choice" in favour of national unity.
articles.body:
People in Alberta have voted overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada, projected results suggest, after residents of the western province were asked in a public ballot whether or not they wanted a referendum at a later date on becoming independent.

With most votes counted, more than two-thirds of voters had chosen to remain part of the country rather than pursue the referendum, according to Elections Alberta .

The outcome was hailed by Prime Minister Mark Carney as "a clear choice" on the part of Albertans.

At a pro-separatist watch party in Edmonton, the hum of upbeat chatter quickly quieted as those present saw the projected results. However, one separatist leader insisted his campaign was not over.

The vote was called earlier this year by the province's leader, Danielle Smith, in response to a public petition. It was seen as a major test of national unity.

Smith herself opposed the separatist push but said the public will for a vote was undeniable. She welcomed the initial results, commenting: "Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada."

In making the case for independence from Canada, many of the separatists said the oil-rich province's economic growth had been stifled by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa.

But those who opposed a breakup - including Carney - called for Canada to present a united front in the face of external pressures, including an ongoing trade war with the United States.

Follow live updates and reaction after vote in Alberta

After overnight vote projections were published by Canadian broadcaster CBC and others, the mood soured among the separatist camp. A pro-independence watch party attended by the BBC packed up quickly, and people went home.

One of the separatist leaders, Jeffrey Rath, struck a defiant tone, however, vowing that "our movement isn't stopping and we're continuing to move forward".

Speaking to the BBC World Service's Newsday programme, Rath, a lawyer based in Calgary, said he saw Monday's vote as a "first step" which had taught the movement some "valuable lessons".

Asked whether his movement would push to keep holding votes on independence until it got the result it wanted, he responded "why not?", and insisted that "the math and the economics" all added up on his side of the argument.

Smith called the vote in response to a grassroots group gathering about 300,000 signatures on a petition that asked for a binding referendum on separation.

The petition was blocked by a judge, saying it failed to consult indigenous First Nations people - however, Smith opted to go ahead with the ballot.

Another group collected signatures for its own petition that opposed separation, which was signed by more than 400,000 people.

The key question on Monday's voting paper asked: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"

Smith said before the vote that if voters chose the first option, a referendum on separation would not be held - at least, not while she was in power.

Despite the projected results, the conversation around Albertan sovereignty is not over.

Separatists leaders have indicated that they plan to push Smith out of power within her United Conservative Party, in the hope of installing a leader who is more sympathetic to their cause.

It is unclear if they have the numbers on their side to do that, but debate around the issue could dominate politics in Alberta for years to come.

Another separatist leader, Mitch Sylvestre, told the BBC on polling day that "a lot of work will have to be done" to curb the appetite for independence if his side did lose.

Canada has grappled with challenges to its unity before. The province of Quebec held two referendums on independence, in 1980 and 1995. Both were unsuccessful, but Alberta separatists believe Quebec used the threat of independence to gain significant political leverage over Canada's central government.

Although responses to the referendum question are being tallied as a priority, there were nine other questions on Monday's ballot paper.

Five of these dealt with immigration, while the other four focused on the Canadian constitution.

articles.body: A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a bug in the company’s San Francisco office was in contact with a member of the Saudi royal family who urged him to return to the kingdom and join its artificial intelligence initiative, prosecutors said, as cited by CBS News.Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national, was arrested on October 9 over allegations that he installed a recording device in a conference room used by OpenAI executives. articles.title: Isle of Man Assisted Dying Bill granted Royal Assent
articles.summary: Assisted dying will become legal on the Isle of Man after being granted approval by Westminster.
articles.body:
The Isle of Man's Assisted Dying Bill has been granted Royal Assent.

The law will allow adults who have lived on the island for at least five years, who have a terminal illness with a life expectancy of 12 months or less, to request an assisted death.

In a statement, campaign group Dignity in Dying said: "The milestone is a tribute to the Manx families who campaigned for years for a change in the law."

But opponents to the bill have said they are "deeply disappointed" at the news.

The island became the first place in the British Isles to pass laws on assisted dying in March 2025, but they needed amendments before Royal Assent could be given.

A similar bill in Jersey was given Royal Assent in July this year.

The chief executive of Dignity in Dying, Sarah Wootten, said: "Today is a historic and deeply emotional day for the Isle of Man, and above all for the families who made it happen."

Dignity in Dying said every request would be subject to "strict eligibility assessments, medical oversight and independent post-death review".

Wootten added: "Dying Manx people now have the reassurance that, if their suffering becomes unbearable, they will not be abandoned to pain, fear or desperate alternatives."

The bill's author, Alex Allinson, a former Ramsey MHK, said: "This is the culmination of decades of campaigning by island residents and their politicians to ensure greater choice, compassion and dignity for those facing a terminal illness."

And Clare Barber, a former environment minister, who supported the bill, added: "Having worked as a nurse, the concept of a good death is one that is exceptionally important to me.

"This does not negate the need for palliative care, it compliments it."

But campaigners against the laws have also spoken up.

In a statement Manx Duty of Care said it was "deeply disappointed" with the announcement, calling for "new members of Tynwald to table a bill to repeal it at once".

The object to the legislation, saying it "clearly breaches the European Convention on Human Rights, the Isle of Man NHS Act and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of People with Disabilities".

articles.title: A small backyard railway started by Oregon hobbyist Ed St John inspired a neighbour to buy surrounding land; after the tracks were joined in 1992, it grew into a 32-mile miniature railroad across 2,200 acres
articles.summary: What began as one man's backyard hobby in Southern Oregon has grown into a sprawling railway landscape where tiny trains travel through thousands of acres.
articles.body: What began as one man's backyard hobby in Southern Oregon has grown into a sprawling railway landscape where tiny trains travel through thousands of acres. According to the official website, Train Mountain is far removed from the idea of a garden railway: its 32 miles of 7.5-inch-gauge track wind across 2,200 acres, creating what the Guinness Book of World Records recognises as the world's longest rideable miniature hobby railway. Scroll down to read its history and what makes it a rare one.A backyard dream takes shapeAccording to the website, the story began with Oregon hobbyist Ed St. John, who started building a railroad in his backyard. His project, called the Over-The-Hill Live Steamers, soon attracted volunteers from nearby Medford. The arrangement was simple: if St. John supplied the materials, enthusiasts were happy to make the journey and help build the railway.The original line eventually became the Klamath and Western loop, preserving the roots of what would become a much larger railway operation.Neighbour Quintin Breen, who had spent much of his life fascinated by trains, soon learned about St. John's project. Rather than simply admire it, Breen began purchasing land next to the existing railroad with an ambitious idea: create a much bigger miniature railway, states the website.In 1992, the two railroads were connected. Breen later acquired St. John's property, bringing the original backyard railway into what would become Train Mountain.From hobby railroad to railway landmarkAs the property expanded, so did the railway. By 2000, the operation had become substantial enough to host a gathering of the International Brotherhood of Live Steamers, an organisation involved in establishing standards and promoting the miniature railway hobby.Nearly 100 trains arrived for that event, revealing the potential of Train Mountain as a destination for railway enthusiasts. Breen eventually developed the idea of making the gathering a recurring event, leading to the Train Mountain Triennial.Held every three years, the meet has grown into a major international gathering. Recent editions have attracted more than 1,000 people, with participants bringing trains from countries including Germany and Australia, explains the website data.A railway built around historyToday, Train Mountain Institute oversees the 2,200-acre property as a nonprofit organisation dedicated to railroad education and history. Its miniature railway stretches for more than 32 miles, while the Train Mountain Museum houses more than 50 full-sized rail cars, maintenance-of-way equipment and other railway artefacts.Visitors can experience the sprawling property from the tracks themselves, travelling aboard trains built at one-eighth scale. Those who prefer a slower exploration can also walk through parts of the grounds.The experience combines the intimacy of a hobby railway with the scale of a major rail museum, turning an enthusiast's backyard experiment into a destination built around the history, mechanics and culture of railroading, adds the website data.Keeping the original spirit aliveThe railway's operation is supported by several nonprofit organisations and a large community of volunteers. Train Mountain Railroad members help maintain the property, operate the museum and organise regular meets, while Train Mountain Institute oversees the broader educational mission.Meanwhile, the Klamath & Western Railroad continues to operate on the original loop created by St. John. During summer Saturdays, it carries on the tradition of offering public rides and operates a small lunch stand.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Strabane: Councillor raises concerns over NI town's UK Town of Culture bid
articles.summary: Independent councillor Paul Gallagher says including 'UK' in the title is problematic, but unionists disagree.
articles.body:
A councillor has voiced concerns over a town in Northern Ireland being considered as the UK's first Town of Culture.

Paul Gallagher, who is an independent councillor in Strabane, County Tyrone, said the inclusion of the word "UK" in the title is problematic for him and some constituents in the mainly-nationalist town.

However, Ulster Unionist councillor Derek Hussey said he could not understand Gallagher's argument, as Strabane clearly is in the United Kingdom.

The town is one of 15 UK locations shortlisted for the inaugural competition run by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport with a prize of £3m up for grabs.

The bid is supported by celebrities such as singer-songwriter Paul Brady and BBC Radio presenter Hugo Duncan, as well as most councillors, including the Sinn Féin Mayor of Derry and Strabane Grace Uí Niallais.

The public have been asked what they would like to see in the final bid, which is due to be submitted by the end of November.

BBC News NI has contacted Derry City and Strabane District Council (DCSDC) for comment.

UK Town of Culture is a new Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) competition.

It said it was inspired by the success of the UK City of Culture - which was won by Londonderry in 2013 - and aims to "celebrate towns and help to create a lasting cultural legacy".

The government will select the best small, medium and large towns from an initial batch of almost 400 applications.

One will be named UK Town of Culture 2028 and receive £3m to develop a year-long programme of cultural celebrations while the other two finalists will each receive £250,000.

Speaking to BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme , Gallagher said the County Tyrone town is "in dire need of investment", but many of his constituents who would have some reservations about the UK title.

"Some people are stating clearly they will not be part of a UK culture bid, so, as an elected representative, I need to be cognisant of that," he said.

"Strabane, it's not only a nationalist town, it's a Republican town, and that needs to be taken on board.

"Lots of money comes in from various sources, from the British Treasury, from a lot of places, but it doesn't come with a condition on it that says you're in the UK."

Councillor Hussey rejected Gallagher's comments and said he "failed to understand" them.

"This is a question of accepting reality," he said.

" I don't want to go back to the Belfast Agreement, but the Belfast Agreements set asides all questions regarding the issue of sovereignty with regard Northern Ireland, until if such times the people here decide otherwise."

Hussey said this conversation could be viewed as "isolating" for people of a British identity in the Strabane area.

"I don't see why an Irish identity cannot be included within a UK Town of Culture because the United Kingdom covers a wide range of identities and nationalities.

"The UK has a multitude of cultures and this bid is a celebration of culture.

"The benefit that could come to the town would be amazing, the top prize, if you want to call it that, is £3m to assist with the development of the overall project and year of cultural events."

articles.title: ‘Scandalous’ to say Ukrainians are dying due to U.S. pulling support, Rubio says
articles.summary: U.S. envoys were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambles to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin.
articles.body: U.S. envoys were expected to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway on Tuesday, as Kyiv scrambles to respond to an American pressure campaign that has been allied with moves aimed at courting the Kremlin. President Donald Trump’s negotiators, son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, have so far had little success finding a diplomatic solution to the war. Their latest meeting comes with Washington’s backing for Kyiv in doubt as Zelenskyy accused the U.S. of withdrawing support crucial to his country’s defense against Russia — a suggestion that Secretary of State Marco Rubio called “scandalous.” Witkoff will be meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on Tuesday, with Kushner joining via videoconference, the Norwegian government said. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb will also join the talks, it added. Officials from the U.S. and Ukraine had been expected to meet in Norway this week for another round of negotiations, sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as a series of recent actions by Trump in favor of Russia left both Congress and U.S. allies questioning U.S. mediation efforts. Trump has waived sanctions and agreed a diesel deal with Russia, in an apparent bid to lower fuel prices ahead of the Midterm elections. He called Monday for Zelenskyy to “get somebody else to negotiate,” his latest rebuke of the Ukrainian president. Trump also appeared to downplay the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine, a near-daily reality for the last 4 ½ years that have killed scores of civilians and flattened towns. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “They haven’t been doing much.” It was the latest public sign of his shift away from Ukraine. Kyiv said it had once again received no early warning from the U.S. before the capital came under attack by Russian ballistic missiles on Sunday, the third time in recent days. In addition to the withholding of intelligence, Ukraine said it was still facing speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the SpaceX service, with no explanation from the American side. “All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” Zelenskyy said Monday in a virtual address to a bipartisan Congressional delegation. He also said the U.S. was delaying the delivery of crucial ballistic missile interceptors. Zelenskyy said early Tuesday he held “a substantive conversation” with Rubio, focusing on missile interceptors, early warnings of ballistic attacks and Starshield restrictions. He thanked Rubio and “everyone in America who supports fair approaches.” Rubio told reporters later that he told Zelenskyy in the 45-minute call that nothing had changed in U.S. support for Ukraine. “There’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he added, speaking at the start of a trip to India. Ukrainian officials including Zelenskyy have made clear their accusation that the U.S. has imposed restrictions that have disrupted military operations and hampered its ability to intercept Russian missiles, making the attacks more deadly. “That’s scandalous, that’s outrageous, that’s just simply not true. That’s not accurate,” Rubio said Tuesday. Officials in the eastern Kharkiv region shared images Monday of a dead child in a stroller — a one-year-old girl they said was killed alongside her mother in a Russian attack on a public park in the region. “The world has enough strength to stop the war. That strength must finally be used — against the murderers,” Zelenskyy said in a post decrying the strike.

articles.title: Myanmar’s detained ex-leader Suu Kyi receives package from King Charles III
articles.summary: Military-backed government says it delivered two books and diplomatic correspondence to Aung San Suu Kyi.
articles.body:
Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has received a package from King Charles III, its military-backed government said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months.

Home ministry officials met the country’s former leader on Monday to deliver the parcel containing two books about soil and sealed diplomatic correspondence from the British monarch, Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page. Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and King Charles is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera. The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicised meeting with a foreign official since she was ousted more than five years ago.

Myanmar authorities referred to Suu Kyi as a “special female prisoner” on Tuesday, the first time they have used the term to describe the pro-democracy and human rights advocate, whose global reputation suffered after she rejected accusations of genocide committed against Myanmar’s Muslim Rohingya minority.

Suu Kyi was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former military government chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

The international community, including Britain, has called for Suu Kyi’s release and access to her as part of efforts to resolve the country’s political crisis, but the government has rejected those calls.

articles.title: Zelensky prepares for Oslo talks with US envoys as Rubio denies withholding intelligence
articles.summary: The US secretary of state rejects accusations Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence.
articles.body:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in Norway ahead of talks with Volodymyr Zelensky with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the meeting with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".

Ahead of the meeting, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected as "scandalous" and "outrageous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.

He was speaking after Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, told the BBC that the lack of reliable US warnings meant lives were being lost.

Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

Støre said the aim of the Oslo talks were to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.

Zelensky said earlier he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.

Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to the Starlink network in Ukraine, and unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors had not yet been approved.

The US secretary of state is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.

Witkoff is expected to be joined by video-link by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, and by several European representatives, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and officials from the UK, Poland, France and Germany, as well as the EU and Nato.

It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after his visit to Oslo, however the Kremlin spokeman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's special envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".

Earlier this month Russia's Vladimir Putin discussed the war with Trump over the phone, and not long afterwards the US president announce that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".

He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden.

"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.

Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".

"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."

articles.title: UK to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks
articles.summary: The United Kingdom said Tuesday it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen.
articles.body: The United Kingdom said Tuesday it will deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen. The UK will fly “defensive counter-air missions” using Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the defense ministry said in a statement. Over the past month, the Houthis have intensified their targets on Saudi Arabia, launching ballistic missiles and drones at key infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, in response to the kingdom’s support for the Yemeni government. “The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable,” UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said in the statement. “The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region.” “This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” he added. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: 25 must-visit destinations for 2027, according to National Geographic
articles.summary: From Luxor, Egypt, to Baltimore, Maryland, these are the places National Geographic thinks you should visit in 2027, and why.
articles.body: It’s too easy to kick the can down the road when planning dream trips: Push it to next month, next year, after the new kitchen is done, or never. To help banish the endless procrastination, National Geographic’s 2027 list of 25 must-visit destinations for the year ahead is one of its most timely and experience-driven recommendations yet. There are new openings, such as the Cape Froward National Park in Chile, and landmark anniversaries, like a Beethoven festival in Leipzig, Germany, to mark the 200th anniversary of the composer’s death. There are cultural celebrations, including an arts festival in Japan’s “Snow Country,” and once-remote locations with improved accessibility, such as Mexico’s Maya Ka’an, now linked to Cancún and Tulum by train. National Geographic’s editor-in-chief, Nathan Lump, talked to CNN about some of the destinations he’s most excited about. Pacific Coast Highway, California California’s Pacific Coast Highway is “probably the most iconic road trip you could take in America, outside of Route 66,” says Lump, and with the beloved Big Sur section now open again after a three-year closure, it’s possible for travelers to enjoy it in its entirety. Lump recommends people explore the thriving creative communities in the towns en route, such as Mendocino and Laguna Beach. California has for a long time attracted “artists inspired by the landscape, by the ocean, and so you really can see that and experience that on display as you make this drive.” Baltimore, Maryland America’s first commercial railroad opened in Baltimore, Maryland, 200 years ago in 1827. To celebrate, the city’s National Museum of Railroad History & Innovation has undergone a $38 million upgrade, culminating in the opening of its future-minded Innovation Hall early next year. “Baltimore is often thought of as a maritime city”, says Lump, but there’s a lot more to Charm City than people often realize. It’s “dynamic and thriving” and “continues to undergo revitalization and change in really positive ways.” Puerto Rico Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl LX halftime performance put Puerto Rico in the international spotlight and, says Lump, “people got a bit more of a taste of its culture.” Much more than just a beach destination, the island’s music, dance and culinary traditions reflect its distinct “blend of African and Indigenous and, of course, Spanish Influences.” Puerto Rico’s Indigenous heritage can be traced along the Taíno Route with its historic settlements, sacred caves and centuries-old rock carvings. Grenada The new year marks the 150th anniversary of Spicemas, the annual August carnival in Grenada, which is known as the Spice Island due to its cultivation of nutmeg, cloves and other scented delights. “It’s a beautiful island, lush and green,” says Lump, and Spicemas is “a great time to go: music, parades, street parties, super fun.” Grenada also offers a wealth of wellness activities, such as volcanic mud bathing at River Sallee and guided yoga sessions at Royal Mount Carmel Falls, one of the island’s tallest waterfalls. Santander, Spain Two world-class art museums are debuting in Santander, on Spain’s northern coast, bringing fresh international attention to this ancient port city. Faro Santander opened last month to display the extensive art collection of Banco Santander, including works by Titian, Velázquez, and Goya. Next year, Madrid’s prestigious Museo Reina Sofía will open an outpost in the city, with a collection of 138,000 paintings, sculptures and manuscripts. “And then they’ve got this great archaeology museum,” says Lump, Santander’s Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology, which is moving to a brand-new, $56 million home designed by prize-winning Barcelona-based architects Mendoza Partida. Kuélap, Chachapoyas, Peru “You’d definitely be the first of your friends to go there if you went,” says Lump of Kuélap, an ancient citadel in northern Peru built by the Chachapoya people around 500 C.E. A new trail set to open in June reaches part of the Malcapampa ruins, a formerly inaccessible archaeological site. Visitors “can observe a live archaeological site as well, and the archeologists that work there, which I think is quite fun and different,” says Lump. Venture beyond Kuélap and hikers can reach sites where one can spot the Chachapoya people’s “human-shaped sarcophagi that contain mummies that are perched on the cliff side,” he says. “It’s very weird and cool.” Luxor, Egypt Luxor, in southern Egypt, will enjoy the longest duration of totality during the solar eclipse that will blot out the sun in parts of Europe, the Middle East and Africa on August 2. “The sun was such an important part of cosmology to the ancient Egyptians” and “of all the places you can go in Egypt and experience” the ancient world, says Lump, Luxor “has probably the densest collection of riches.” The historic Winter Palace hotel, where Howard Carter announced the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922, is due to reopen in July as the Mandarin Oriental Winter Palace. Nile cruises, such as the legendary Steam Ship Sudan which inspired Agatha Christie’s “Death on the Nile,” are a “wonderful” way to see the region, but in 2027 travelers will also have the option of riding on Egypt’s first luxury tourist sleeper train, the Guardian of the Nile. It will link Cairo and Aswan with a stop in Luxor.
